title: CAP Theorem Simplified _ System Design Fundamentals

segments.text: What is cap theorem? How useful is it to system design? Let's take a look. The cap theorem
is a concept in computer science that explains the trade-offs between consistency, availability,
and partition tolerance in distributed systems. Consistency refers to the property of a
system where all nodes have a consistent view of the data. It means all clients see the same data
at the same time, no matter which note they connect to. Availability refers to the ability
of a system to respond to requests from users at all times. Partition tolerance refers to the
ability of a system to continue operating even if there is a network partition. But what is a
network partition? A network partition happens when nodes in a distributed system are
enabled to communicate with each other due to network failures. When there is a network partition,
a system has choose between consistency and availability. If the system prioritizes consistency,
it may become unavailable until the partition is resolved. If the system prioritizes availability,
it may allow updates to the data. This could result in data in consistencies until the partition is resolved.
Now let's go through a concrete example. Let's say with a tiny bang with two ATM's connected
over the network. The ATM supports three operations, deposit, withdraw, and check balance.
No matter what happens, the balance should never go below zero. There is no central database
in this bang to keep the account balance. It is stored on both ATM's. When a customer uses an ATM,
the balance is updated on both ATM's over the network. This ensures that the ATM's
have a consistent view of their account balance. If there is a network partition and the ATM's
are enabled to communicate with each other, the system has choose between consistency and
an availability. If the bang prioritizes consistency, the ATM may refuse to process deposits
of withdraws until the partition is resolved. This ensures that the balance remains consistent,
but the system is unavailable to customers. If the bang prioritizes availability, the ATM may
allow deposits and withdraws to occur, but the balance may become inconsistent until the partition
is resolved. When there is a network partition, the customer could withdraw the entire balance
from both ATM's. When the network comes back online, the inconsistencies is resolved and now the
balance is negative. That is not good. Now let's go through another example and see how a social
media platform could apply the kept theorem. During a network partition, if two users are commenting
on the same pose at the same time, one users comment may not be visible to the other users
until the partition is resolved. Alternatively, if the platform prioritizes consistency,
the commenting feature may be unavailable to users until the partition is resolved.
For a social network, it is often acceptable to prioritize availability at the cost of users
seeing slightly different views some of the time. The kept theorem may sound very simple,
but the real world is messy. As with many things in software engineering, this is all about trade-offs
and the choices are not always so black and white. The kept theorems assumes 100% availability
or 100% consistency. In the real world, there are degrees of consistency and availability.
That distributed system designers must carefully consider. This is where the simplistic model
of the kept theorem could be misleading. Now back to the bank example. During the a network
partition, the ATM could allow only balance inquiries to be processed while it deposits and withdraws
a blocked. Alternatively, the bank could implement a hybrid approach. For example, the ATM could
allow balance inquiries and small withdraws to be processed during a partition, but block
large withdraws and all deposits until the partition is resolved. This worth noting that in the real
world, reconciliation after a network partition could get very messy. The bank example above
is simple to reconcile. In real life, the data structures involved could be complex and challenging
to reconcile. A good example of a complex data structure is Google Docs,
resolving conflicting updates could be tricky. So is the kept theorem useful? Yes, it is a useful tool
to help us things through the high-level trade-offs to consider when there is a network partition.
This is a good starting point, but it does not provide a complete picture of the trade-offs
to consider when designing a well-rounded distributed system. Specifically, when the system is
operating normally without a network failure, which is most of the time, there is an entire set
of interesting trade-offs to consider between latency and consistency. This is covered by the
pack-held theorem, which we should cover in another video. You would like to learn more about
system design, check out our books and weekly newsletter. Please subscribe if you learned something
new. Thank you so much and we'll see you next time.
